Definition: Affordability of mobile broadband data, measured as the cost of a basic mobile data plan (1-2GB) as a percentage of GNI per capita. The UN Broadband Commission target is below 2% of monthly GNI per capita. Affordability is the single largest barrier to internet adoption in Africa.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: A light check surfaced a plausible figure, so this row was escalated from the fast path. USAID's Digital Development mAccess diagnostic tool records Liberia's entry-level 1GB mobile prepaid basket at approximately 3.3% of GNI per capita, which falls in the 'Moderate (2-5%)' band rather than confirming Unknown. This is corroborated contextually by ITU's finding that mobile data baskets across Africa typically cost 3-7% of GNI per capita, but the mAccess figure is a single aggregator source of uncertain vintage (page last updated 2023, underlying data likely ~2022) rather than a primary ITU/A4AI country data point, so the exact tier should be checked against a primary ITU IPB or A4AI dataset before treating as final.
revised_comments: Liberia's entry-level (1GB) mobile broadband basket costs an estimated 3.3% of GNI per capita, placing it in the moderate affordability band. This is broadly consistent with ITU regional data showing mobile data baskets across Africa typically cost between 3% and 7% of GNI per capita.

Definition: The country's total international internet bandwidth capacity per internet user, indicating the quality and capacity of the country's connection to the global internet. Determined by submarine cable landings (for coastal states), cross-border terrestrial fibre (for landlocked states), and satellite links.

revision_notes: A light check surfaced usable data, so this row was escalated from the fast path. USAID's Digital Development mAccess tool records Liberia's international bandwidth per user at approximately 14.8 kbit/s, and a secondary aggregator citing ITU data shows an older (2016) value of 6.31 kbit/s per user — both fall in the 'Low (5-19 kbit/s)' band. Liberia depends on a single submarine cable landing (ACE) with no major reported capacity upgrade that would push it into the next band, but neither source is a primary ITU dataset with a firm recent year, so the vintage is uncertain.
revised_comments: Liberia's international internet bandwidth per user is estimated at around 15 kbit/s, placing it in the 'Low' band. The country depends on a single international submarine cable connection point (the ACE cable, landing via the Cable Consortium of Liberia), which constrains available capacity relative to internet users.

Definition: Whether the country has an operational Internet Exchange Point (IXP) and its maturity. IXPs enable local internet traffic to be exchanged domestically rather than being routed internationally, reducing latency, costs, and dependence on foreign infrastructure. Critical for local digital ecosystem development.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: A light check surfaced a clearly authoritative source, so this row was escalated from the fast path and the score corrected from 'no IXP found' to reflect an active IXP. The Packet Clearing House global IXP directory lists the Liberia Internet Exchange Point (LIXP) in Monrovia as Active. A February 2025 news report and a Liberia Telecommunications Authority (LTA) statement confirm LIXP is Liberia's sole IXP, hosted by the Cable Consortium of Liberia, recently received $39,000 of upgraded equipment, but still has limited participation from ISPs and mobile operators, who are not all peering at the exchange.
revised_comments: Liberia has one operational Internet Exchange Point, the Liberia Internet Exchange Point (LIXP) in Monrovia, hosted by the Cable Consortium of Liberia and listed as active in the Packet Clearing House global IXP directory. The Liberia Telecommunications Authority has invested in upgraded equipment, but participation remains limited, with governance challenges and incomplete peering among ISPs and mobile network operators noted at a 2025 National Peering Forum.

Definition: Whether the country has enacted legal or regulatory requirements mandating that certain categories of data (personal data, government data, financial data, or critical infrastructure data) be stored within national borders. Central to data sovereignty debates in Africa.
redteam_note: No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: The cited DLA Piper source was fetched and re-read in full. It confirms Liberia has no comprehensive, cross-sectoral data protection or localisation law, supporting the general thrust of the original 'No data localisation requirements' score, but the same DLA Piper page also documents a sectoral localisation requirement in the financial sector: Section 9(c) of the Central Bank of Liberia's E-Payment Regulation states that e-payment systems 'should be hosted locally... however, if the system is hosted in another jurisdiction, licensed institutions shall ensure that the information requested are provided promptly and that the CBL has unfettered access.' This meets the definition of a sectoral (financial-sector) localisation/access requirement, so the score is corrected upward from 1 (No requirements) to 3 (Sectoral requirements only). A 2024/2025 draft National Data Governance Policy and a proposed Personal Data Protection and Privacy Act would introduce broader localisation and classification rules but remain unenacted.
revised_comments: Liberia has no comprehensive, economy-wide data localisation law, but a sectoral requirement applies to electronic payments: the Central Bank of Liberia's E-Payment Regulation (Section 9(c)) requires e-payment systems to be hosted locally, or, if hosted abroad, requires that the Central Bank retain unfettered access to system data and reports. A draft National Data Governance Policy and a proposed Personal Data Protection and Privacy Act, which would introduce broader localisation and data classification requirements, remain unenacted as of 2024-2025.

Definition: The gap between urban and rural electricity access rates. A smaller gap indicates more equitable energy distribution, critical for ensuring ICT infrastructure can serve the whole population, not just cities.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: A light check surfaced clear World Bank World Development Indicators figures, so this row was escalated from the fast path. World Bank data (indicators EG.ELC.ACCS.UR.ZS and EG.ELC.ACCS.RU.ZS) show urban electricity access of 52.7% in 2023 versus rural access of 9.3% in 2023, a gap of approximately 43 percentage points, which falls in the 41-60pp band rather than Unknown. A separate World Bank Multi-Tier Framework household survey (using Tier 0/no-access shares) shows a similar-sized gap (92.2% of rural households versus 59.5% of urban households with no electricity access at all), corroborating the scale of the divide.
revised_comments: World Bank data show 52.7% of Liberia's urban population had access to electricity in 2023, compared with 9.3% of the rural population, a gap of approximately 43 percentage points. This places Liberia in the 41-60 percentage point gap band, reflecting a strongly urban-concentrated electricity grid alongside limited rural off-grid coverage.
